strengths: Significant dataset contribution: 661K frames (9× larger than prior mmWave HMR dataset mmBody), with high-quality marker-based MoCap annotations addressing ground-truth bias in prior work

Novel dual-modality radar representation: First dataset providing both raw radar tensors (RT) and processed point clouds (RPC) for HMR; empirical results validate RT's superior generalization (S2/S3 cross-subject/action)

Comprehensive experimental design: Multiple protocols (in-place, sit-in-place, non-in-place), evaluation splits (random, cross-subject, cross-action), metrics (MVE, MJE, MRE, TE), and multimodal comparisons
Diverse and practical action set: 50 actions spanning daily activities, rehabilitation exercises, and sports support multiple application domains (elderly care, healthcare, VR)

Technical rigor in system design: Precise calibration methodology, time synchronization protocol, effective RPC ratio analysis demonstrating human-centric radar advantage, high-resolution Vayyar sensor (7 GHz BW, 20 Tx/Rx)
Insightful scaling analysis: Figure 5 demonstrates scaling laws hold for mmWave HMR; larger datasets improve performance on generalization splits (S2/S3)
First RT-based HMR baseline: RT-Mesh addresses algorithmic gap in processing raw radar tensors; pragmatic two-stage design achieves 2.74ms latency
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: RT-Mesh employs straightforward components (2D BEV convolution/transformer + 3D RoI + HMR head) with no ablation studies or justification of architectural choices; acknowledged as 'simple baseline' limiting research contribution

Inadequate analysis of persistent generalization challenges: Cross-subject (S2) and cross-action (S3) performance remain poor despite 9× dataset scale (90.9mm → 135.1mm MVE, 48.5% increase); root causes not deeply investigated beyond identifying self-occlusion and multipath

Insufficient error analysis and failure mode investigation: No per-body-part error breakdown, systematic failure mode study, or investigation of body-part miss-detection; limited qualitative examples (Fig. 6) without comprehensive analysis

Concerning downstream task results: Table 4 shows dramatic HAR degradation (GT: 75.67% → RT: 61.06% Top-1, S1; cross-subject: 27.85%), raising questions about practical mesh quality despite acceptable MVE metrics

Incomplete robustness evaluation: Missing sensitivity analysis for calibration errors, justification for temporal context (T=4 frames), statistical significance testing (no confidence intervals), and evaluation on multi-person/occluded scenarios
Shallow multimodal fusion exploration: Only intermediate feature fusion tested; no attention-based alignment, cross-modal learning, or investigation of why fusion helps S1/S3 more than S2

Questionable computational efficiency claims: RT-Mesh vs RT-Pose latency comparison somewhat unfair (different full-volume processing strategies); throughput and memory consumption not reported; edge device deployment claims unsupported

Dataset balance and bias concerns: Unclear distribution of 661K frames across 50 actions and 20 subjects; potential subject-specific overfitting not addressed; limited subject diversity (20 subjects, similar to mmBody)

Reproducibility constraints: Supplementary materials unavailable for review; dataset/code release conditional rather than immediate; some hyperparameter choices (RoI size, loss weights) lack justification

Practical deployment gap: High-quality annotations require marker suits; generalization without marker supervision at test time not discussed; cross-hardware portability (specific Vayyar + RealSense) unclear

strengths: Significant scale advance: 661K frames is 9× larger than prior mmWave-based HMR datasets (mmBody), with high-fidelity marker-based MoCap annotations avoiding pseudo-GT bias
Novel dataset contribution: First benchmark supporting both raw radar tensors (RT) and processed radar point clouds (RPC) for HMR, enabling research across RF signal granularities
Comprehensive multimodal evaluation: Thorough benchmarking across modalities (RGB, depth, RPC, RT), three split protocols (random, cross-subject, cross-action), and downstream tasks (HAR, HMP)
Rigorous data acquisition pipeline: Careful calibration (PnP-based), time synchronization, and three-stage annotation with SOMA reconstruction and human verification
Diverse action set: 50 actions spanning daily activities, rehabilitation, and sports, supporting multiple real-world applications (healthcare, VR/AR, robotics)
Practical data engineering: RT-LMDB system effectively addresses I/O bottleneck, reducing data loading time from >18h to <1h per epoch for large-scale training
First RT-based HMR baseline: RT-Mesh demonstrates feasibility of direct raw tensor processing with competitive efficiency (2.74ms latency, 2.6 GFLOPs)
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-organized paper with detailed system description, supplementary implementation details, and promise of public release
weaknesses: Poor generalization to unseen subjects/actions: Significant performance degradation from S1→S2 (48% increase) and S1→S3 (57% increase in MVE); limited analysis of failure modes or mitigation strategies
Persistent performance gap vs. RGB-D: Depth modality outperforms radar by 24-25% across splits; non-in-place actions remain highly challenging (142mm MVE), questioning practical applicability

Limited technical novelty: RT-Mesh uses straightforward 2D-then-3D design without temporal modeling despite T=4 frame windows; competing methods mostly adapt existing HPE methods with minimal algorithmic innovation

Weak downstream task performance: HAR cross-action accuracy collapses to 27.85% Top-1 (vs. 75.67% S1), raising questions about mesh quality and downstream utility; results relegated to supplementary without analysis

Methodological concerns: Manual head-swing synchronization trigger is ad-hoc; synchronization error bounds not reported; Vicon-frame temporal matching introduces ~41ms potential misalignment; annotation error propagation unquantified

Limited generalization analysis: Only 20 subjects with no demographic/age diversity analysis; unclear why 9× larger dataset does not substantially close RGB-D gap; no investigation of transfer learning improvements
Overstated privacy claims: De-identification via masks is weak; radar still encodes identifiable information (gait, body shape); no formal privacy analysis or differential privacy guarantees provided

Incomplete validation: No calibration accuracy validation (e.g., reprojection error); SOMA reconstruction error not quantified; evaluation favors pose over shape accuracy; single-run results without significance testing
Scope limitations: Single indoor environment (6×5.5m²), proprietary Vayyar hardware with unclear transfer to other platforms, no validation on synthetic data or external datasets
Missing ablations and analysis: No multi-path interference studies, CFAR parameter sensitivity analysis, failure case characterization, or ablation on LMDB compression impact

strengths: Substantial dataset scale (661K frames, 9× larger than prior work) with high-quality marker-based MoCap annotations verified through human-in-the-loop cleanup
Comprehensive multimodal design providing both raw radar tensors (RT) and processed point clouds (RPC), enabling research at different signal processing levels
Diverse action coverage (50 actions spanning daily, rehabilitation, and sports activities) with rigorous evaluation across multiple protocols and generalization splits
Well-engineered data infrastructure including RT-LMDB system for efficient I/O (reduces epoch time from >18h to <1h) and careful cross-modal calibration
Extensive benchmarking demonstrating complementary value of RT and RPC modalities through fusion experiments
weaknesses: Critical generalization gap undermines dataset utility: cross-subject generalization shows 48% error increase (90.9→135.1mm MVE), raising fundamental questions about whether the dataset is sufficient for learning robust models

Unfair comparison with vision methods: RGB baseline (TokenHMR) uses large-scale AMASS pretraining while radar methods train from scratch; pretraining improves RGB by 50%, confounding modality comparisons

Minimal technical novelty: RT-Mesh is a straightforward two-stage architecture (2D BEV localization + 3D RoI regression) with standard loss functions; no ablation studies, comparison with end-to-end approaches, or architectural innovation

Insufficient analysis of fundamental challenges: paper acknowledges poor generalization, body-shape estimation errors, and performance drops for sit-in-place actions but provides only superficial explanations without investigation or solutions

Weak support for RT>RPC claims: superiority claimed without analyzing what information CFAR filtering removes, which body parts benefit, or visualization of information loss; differences are modest in some metrics

Limited dataset scope inadequately discussed: only 20 subjects (small by modern standards), single indoor location, constrained distance range (2-4m optimal per Fig. 14), curated actions without real-world variability, specific to one radar hardware
Privacy claims lack rigor: no formal privacy analysis, threat modeling, or re-identification risk evaluation; claims sound marketing-oriented rather than empirically grounded
Downstream task evaluation shows poor generalization: HAR performance collapses in cross-subject setting (59.91%→27.85% Top-1 accuracy), demonstrating intermediate representations don't transfer well

Reproducibility concerns: dataset URL missing in submission, code availability unclear, hyperparameters chosen empirically without justification or sensitivity analysis, no significance testing or confidence intervals

Missing ablation studies and temporal analysis: no justification for T=4 frame window, no sensitivity analysis for architecture choices, no temporal consistency metrics or analysis of motion speed effects

strengths: Significant dataset contribution: 661K frames (9× larger than prior largest radar HMR dataset) with high-quality marker-based MoCap annotations
Dual-modality radar data (raw tensors and point clouds) at different signal granularity levels, enabling diverse research directions
Superior sensing hardware (Vayyar radar with 7 GHz bandwidth, 20 Tx/Rx) with quantified advantages over automotive radars
Comprehensive benchmarking with multiple protocols (P1-P3), splits (S1-S3), metrics (MVE, MJE, MRE, TE), and multimodal fusion analysis
First HMR method operating on raw radar tensors (RT-Mesh) with efficient two-stage architecture achieving competitive performance at 2.74ms latency
Diverse action set (50 actions spanning daily, rehabilitation, sports) supporting multiple applications
Privacy-preserving sensing application addressing real-world deployment concerns without appearance information
Rigorous technical execution with careful calibration, synchronization, human-in-the-loop annotation verification, and efficient LMDB-based data handling
weaknesses: Limited subject diversity: only 20 subjects with modest anthropometric variation (1.5-1.8m height, 45-90kg), potentially constraining generalization to diverse populations
Severe generalization challenges: 48% (S2) and 57% (S3) performance degradation in cross-subject/action settings, undermining practical real-world deployment where unseen scenarios are common
Non-in-place dynamic actions remain extremely challenging (178.2mm MVE on S3 vs. 142.0mm for in-place), with limited analysis of failure modes

RT-Mesh baseline is relatively simple despite novelty; lacks temporal modeling despite T=4 frames, with authors acknowledging future work needed for 'higher spatial precision and temporal consistency'
Missing critical analysis: no per-body-part error breakdown, no inter-observer reliability studies for annotation verification, limited quantification of mesh annotation error from SOMA conversion
Method comparison issues: baseline methods adapted from HPE rather than designed for HMR; simple concatenation used for multimodal fusion without sophisticated cross-modal alignment

Practical deployment barriers: Vayyar radar is expensive and not widely available (unlike commodity TI/Qualcomm radars); dataset collection requires specialized Vicon system, limiting reproducibility and community adoption
Limited temporal analysis: T=4 frames at 12Hz (0.33s window) may be insufficient for complex dynamics without justification; no frame-level confidence estimates or temporal smoothness evaluation
Incomplete experimental validation: hyperparameters chosen 'empirically' without systematic ablation studies; no sensitivity analysis or cross-system robustness evaluation

Unaddressed technical depths: CFAR filtering information loss not quantified, optimal sensing range of 2-4m limits practical scenarios, self-occlusion effects in dynamic movements not explicitly addressed
